webpage.text:
Cheap meat and tales of exploitation behind the chicken shop counter | Food & drink industry

Food hygiene inspectors are concerned to find a fully made-up bed on the floor of a small, windowless room behind the busy kitchen of Sam's Great Tasting Chicken, a fast-food outlet in an east London high street. The bed has no mattress, just a sleeping bag laid on top of a couple of dirty blue blankets and neatly turned down sheets.

It is past midnight, and the fried chicken shop is still busy, with customers but the raid by 15 officials from local and central government departments has taken the shop supervisor by surprise and he has to get dressed quickly to answer questions. In this room, tucked beside the walk-in freezer, he has all his belongings to hand: clothes, suitcases, medicine, videos, cologne, shampoos, towels drying on a radiator; he has arranged miniature statues of a leopard, dogs and owls on every available surface to cheer the place up.

The hygiene officials are joined by tax officers who ask him if he's living in the restaurant. He denies it categorically, but can't remember where he lives and struggles to come up with a plausible postal address. "Woodford maybe."

"Do you not know your address?" one of the inspectors asks him. "You must know your address."

"Fifty-eight, isn't it?" the man asks.

Stocked with cheap, imported chicken pieces that are fried and served with chips through the night at low prices, these shops are growing in number in Britain's high streets. They are popular with the young but increasingly unpopular with local councils, who are concerned that the cheapness of the food on sale is reflected in employees' working conditions.

Newham council is working with the UK Border Agency, the police, tax inspectors and the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) to crack down on what they suspect to be widespread exploitation of staff at chicken shops throughout the borough.

As a result of 19 raids in the past few months, the council has launched 20 national minimum-wage investigations. "We came across one chicken shop where the pay was £1 an hour. To be fair, they gave the workers some free accommodation – a mattress at the back of the shop, with three of them taking turns on it," Sir Robin Wales, the mayor of Newham, says. "These people are desperate, just trying to do the best for themselves, but the people who employ them should be in prison. It's outrageous, lots of people are being exploited."

Newham council has long been aware that there is chronic underpayment of staff and a huge problem with working conditions at the hundreds of chicken shops in this east London borough, which next month will be one of the Olympic hosts.

But the council does not have the power to mount raids on suspicion of non-payment of the minimum wage. Instead, it has had to couple wage investigations with hygiene checks – because it has the right to enforce health and safety regulations – or to persuade central government tax inspectors to co-ordinate joint investigations.


Careful planning

During a recent raid, 30 officials split into two teams of 15 to mount evening raids on aroundabout 16 shops. The itinerary has been carefully planned to stop staff fleeing premises at one end of the high street when they see shops being raided at the other, but the evening is nevertheless hampered by managers suddenly pulling down the metal shutters over shop fronts and declaring businesses closed for the night.

Before the teams set off, a police officer warns: "These are chicken shops; there will be knives in them as part of their trade, so just be wary." Staff from the DWP benefit fraud team are wearing black protective anti-stab vests.

At Sam's Great Tasting Chicken (which advertises itself to passers-by with a huge lit-up cartoon chicken's head, wearing a cowboy hat and a bow-tie), the dozen teenage customers buying chicken pieces are dismayed and excited to see inspectors arrive at half past midnight, and exclaim: "What the fuck! What the fuck!" An employee coolly continues to serve people fried chicken pieces as the officials file past him to the back of the kitchen.

The inspectors ask the supervisor why, if he isn't living here, there are piles of letters addressed to him at this address. "How long have you lived here?" His English is not very good, but he explains he has moved here from Pakistan 14 years ago. "You must know your address then."

"He has all the comforts of home here. I can't accept that he is just staying the night here," an inspector says.

The man says he is paid £300 a week to work here as a supervisor, he thinks over 12 hours a day, seven days a week, which if right would work out at a rate considerably below the national minimum wage of £6.08 per hour.

He rummages around in a plastic bag, where he keeps his papers, folded in small paper chip bags (decorated with the Sam's Great Tasting Chicken logo, "number one for quality and price"), but he is unable to find any payslips. "OK baby, I will fax it," he tells one of the officials, to her considerable surprise.

This is not the first evidence of staff being accommodated on site. In another chicken shop visited by inspectors, food hygiene staff discover a folded camp bed, made up with blankets inside, next to a cooking stove where a vat of burnt curry is cooling down, in a store room behind the main kitchen. The owner of the establishment says he is keeping the bed there temporarily for the neighbours, but the inspectors express scepticism.

At Fat Chaps (Best Turkish Cuisine), a middle-aged man from Uzbekistan is serving chips over the counter; the air hangs heavy with the smell of frying, and the floor is slippery with grease. A sign behind him reads: "Please do not ask for credit as a smack in the mouth often offends."

Border Agency staff ask the man for his name and passport details, and phone through the information to an immigration call centre, where officials working through the night discover that his student visa was refused in 2009. "You will have to come with us to the police station tonight. You're under arrest for overstaying your visa," a police officer tells him.

They walk upstairs with him to a bare room above the shop, where he changes out of his yellow Fat Chaps T-shirt into jeans that he takes from a suitcase under his bed, and he is taken, without protest, to the police station. A few days later he is deported.

Officials ask the cafe's manager how much the staff are paid. He suggests, hesitantly, £5.80 an hour, and admits that he doesn't know the minimum wage rate. On the other side of the cafe, another cook says he thinks he is paid about £4 an hour. Throughout the evening, employees are very clear about the prices they charge for the chicken meal deals they serve, but peculiarly vague about their own pay arrangements.

At Mighty Chicken and Ribs, at around midnight, the extractor fan is not working, the tables are unwiped and grimy, and rubbish is exploding from the bin. The only member of staff on duty, a student from Pakistan, is also unable to give precise details about his pay arrangements, and claims not to know how to contact his employer. Inspectors tell him off for leaving a half-eaten burger (his supper) behind the till and for storing the chicken on top of the bread in the freezer, along with the day's takings (wrapped in a plastic bag). "You can't keep money in the freezer." Border Agency staff check his student visa, which they report is about to expire.


Complicity

A study into the prevalence of minimum wage abuses recently commissioned by Newham and carried out by Mori and the local charity Community Links pointed out that employees are often "actively complicit in hiding their employers' malpractice because they want to protect their jobs".

It is uncomfortable that the people most alarmed by the night of chicken shop raids are the employees: young teenage brothers from Pakistan who are obliged to show inspectors their living quarters above the shop, students from Bangladesh, who watch with growing unease as border officials check their papers. The shop owners are largely absent, and may receive notification of further action by post later.

Sheila Roberts, the borough enforcement manager,, who has participated in a number of raids, says one employee was so frightened by their arrival that he went to hide in a freezer. She argues that the action has to be taken because employers who do not pay the minimum wage are often violating other regulations, and their staff may not feel able to report injuries or problems.

There are hundreds of chicken shops in Newham, and although some of them do operate legitimate businesses, inspectors say it is rare to visit one and not find some kind of irregularity. The raids are partly an attempt to clear the area before the Olympics, she says: "We don't want visitors to come to Newham and have negative experiences." More importantly, officials "don't want Newham's residents to be exploited", she says. "These are vulnerable people."

Sir Robin Wales has no affection for chicken shops. "There's too many chicken shops; there's too much litter; they attract problems. But the main thing is they're selling really, really cheap chicken to kids," he says. To be able to sell such cut-price food, "very cheap, poor quality chicken" is used and employees are paid very little.

"Good employers are finding it hard to compete. Why should people who are paying the minimum wage have to compete with these people? It makes sense for us to cut out this exploitation of people. While a raid like this will be difficult for those people [who are being exploited], ultimately if we catch people who don't pay the national minimum wage, then we can stop it. You have to do it."

🍗🔥 Top 10 Best Fried Chicken Spots in London

Crispy, juicy, spicy, Korean-style, Nashville hot or classic buttermilk — London’s fried chicken scene is seriously good. If you’re looking for your next chicken fix, these spots deserve a place on your list.

📌 Save this for your next food adventure in London.

1️⃣ Butchies Victoria

📍 SW1E 5NE

Famous for its buttermilk fried chicken burgers, loaded fries and perfectly crispy coating.

2️⃣ Coqfighter Soho

📍 W1F 9SS

One of London’s most popular fried chicken brands, known for creative burgers and bold flavours.

3️⃣ CheeMC Soho ( ft.Karaoke)

📍 W1D 7LR

A must-visit for Korean fried chicken lovers, serving crispy wings and addictive sauces.

4️⃣ Fowl by the Fallow Chefs

📍 SW1Y 4RJ

Elevated fried chicken from the team behind Fallow, with some of the best chicken burgers in Central London.

5️⃣ Thunderbird Fried Chicken - Charing Cross

📍 WC2N 6ND

Known for huge wings, spicy sauces and American-inspired fried chicken.

6️⃣ Good Friend Chicken

📍 WC2H 7JJ

Legendary Taiwanese popcorn chicken that regularly attracts queues in Chinatown.

7️⃣ Monga Fried Chicken (Soho)

📍 W1D 5LL

Taiwanese-style giant fried chicken cutlets packed with flavour and crunch.

8️⃣ Dave’s Hot Chicken

📍 W1D 7ER

The famous Nashville hot chicken spot bringing serious heat to London’s fried chicken scene.

9️⃣ Peck Peck

📍 E8 1HA

Korean-inspired fried chicken with excellent sauces and generous portions.

🔟 Lucky’s Hot Chicken | Seven Dials Market

📍 WC2H 9AU

Serving Nashville-style hot chicken with varying spice levels for every heat tolerance.

✨ Whether you’re craving Korean fried chicken, Taiwanese popcorn chicken, Nashville hot chicken or classic buttermilk burgers, these are some of London’s top-rated chicken spots.

👇 Which one is your favourite?

webpage.text:
The Business Of The Chicken: 12 hours in Chicken Bazooka

It’s late; you’re drunk; in town. Kicking-out time on Lime Street. Neither booze nor romance remains on the cards – and the last 86 has already juddered up Renshaw Street. It’s at this point you might do something you’d never do sober, something perhaps inadvisable, possibly shameful. You might just head into a takeaway, slap down some of your hard-earned and gorge on something objectively, well, filthy. With piping hot chicken hanging from your mouth you blow steam across the packed restaurant and ponder how you’ve ended up – alongside dozens of other fellow revellers – in a fast-food outlet rejoicing in the unlikely name Chicken Bazooka.

For many, such a hazy memory may be their only interaction with Chicken Bazooka; for others, it’s a ritual. For me, it bookends my time in Liverpool. I went there as a callow youth when I first arrived in the city in 1997; 28 years later I found myself back there, pondering the same menu, furniture and greasy aroma of frying animal as when Tony Blair was Prime Minister, Paul McGann was Doctor Who and fully ten million fewer people lived in the UK. I’d decided that spending a day in the venerable takeaway – whose longevity suggests it could survive a nuclear blast – was the best way to understand this peculiarly Liverpudlian edifice; to get to grips with a place whose name implies a violent interface with poultry. I would spend twelve hours in Chicken Bazooka and emerge, hardened of artery and plumper of stomach, with either an appreciation, an understanding or an uneasy truce with one of Liverpool’s most fascinating institutions.


Why? Because while Liverpudlians may not love the food in Chicken Bazooka, they adore the idea of it. Reviews online swing between gratitude and horror. “Honestly,” wrote one woman, “the food tasted like chicken sick – but after a drunk night on the lash, it was all I needed.”

Chicken Bazooka is the sort of place Reddit threads warn you about – a venue that leaves people “very regretful,” once even dubbed “hell on Earth.” Still, the comments keep coming: “Lamb Flavoured Inner Tubing,” “It’s dry & has smell of an old-Englishman” (no, me neither). Others, however, are more generous: “Liverpool’s whimsical weapon against hunger truly delivers,” reads one poetic endorsement. There’s a shitposting Instagram account called chickenbazooka_incellectuals, essentially a fan account for the place. Perhaps it’s the name – a name that provokes laughter the first time it’s heard and a fond roll of the eyes on recollection. Somehow, it remains a place people return to, recommend, and – against all odds – still need.

Although Chicken Bazooka is unique to Liverpool, the fetishisation of fried chicken joints isn’t. The internet hums with Chicken Shop Dates and Chicken Shop Peng. A popular Scouse TikToker once asked locals where to find the best “chicken and can of Coke” (apparently a thing) in Liverpool, as if enquiring about the best cacio e pepe in Rome. The answer, inevitably, was Chicken Bazooka. He went. They forgot his chips. They had no Coke. He didn’t like the chicken. Ho hum.

But the jokes and bad reviews miss the point. Chicken Bazooka was never a great place to eat; there’s plenty of other fried chicken – better fried chicken (Free State Kitchen gets my vote) – in the city. Yet to understand Liverpool you might need to understand Chicken Bazooka: the chaos, the camaraderie, the community. It’s the kind of establishment where a man walks in and asks for a “vegetarian chicken meal,” grinning as though he’s delivered the punchline to a joke no one asked to hear. Where the woman in pyjamas demands mayonnaise from The Big Tupperware (whence it is free, as opposed to the 50p containers – she’s got the cheat codes). Where groups of men and women flirt over a Chickkatito Pizza and Sprite.


There’s a rhythm to the place and a soundtrack. In and out come the people, forever onwards to an ultimate destination. Chicken Bazooka is only ever a stop-off, a detour. At lunchtime, students from Africa and the Middle East drift down the hill from Liverpool’s colleges and unis and pile in. One leaves behind a lanyard. I hand it to the man behind the counter as I order my first Chicken Bazooka of the day and he studies it. “He’s in every day,” he shrugs; we exchange some pleasantries. Then, spreading his hands wide and with the solemnity of a hashish deal in a Moroccan café, he announces: “Now – to the business of the chicken.”

Ah yes, the business of the chicken. Among the 100-odd items on the menu – mainly chicken, admittedly – are delights such as Skittles milkshakes, “Bun” (£1) and a fifteen-piece Bazooka Family Bucket Meal – a poultry Armageddon for ‘four to six’ souls. As I swiftly learn, there’s a kind of chicken roulette to be played – it’s sometimes dry, sometimes damp, often shamefully compelling. Sometimes the chicken is fresh out of the fryer and it’s pretty damn good; at other times it resides, like a Prin in a tanning salon, slowly desiccating under heat lamps. On this occasion I’ve hit the jackpot – two fried thighs, crispy and moist in all the right places, glistening with peppery fat. Is this an outlier? And, if so, what is the reason behind Chicken Bazooka’s endurance?

Outside, the baroque despair of the Adelphi looms, the Broadway Malyan building (officially one of the ugliest buildings in the UK) sulks and Lime Street collides with Mount Pleasant. Chicken Bazooka’s position at this grimy crossroads is surely part of its secret. Surrounded by vape-shop neon, bad-karaoke hangouts and betting-shop grot, it sits at the city’s epicentre, drawing in tourists, commuters and students alike. Many probably come to the city by bus or train and never quite escape the gravity of this dismal quarter. Flanked by two bad hotels – the Scylla and Charybdis of Liverpool hostelry – Lime Street feels like a crummy sentence in Liverpool’s story, with Chicken Bazooka as the full stop. Like the city itself, it’s complicated, but for a fast-food outlet, Ranelagh Place must be a sort of fried-chicken location nirvana.


Inside, it’s all chrome and glass, evoking a 1950s American restaurant that’s been microwaved. A faded image of a once-bustling diner hangs like a Turin shroud of fried fowl. Another sign promises an ISO 9001 quality-certified doner kebab – “the only one in the world.” I don’t doubt it.

Yet beneath the faded glister and parody lies something social, even communal. Like Nabzy’s or Hot’n’Tender, Chicken Bazooka offers halal food, and by day it’s a hub for Liverpool’s Muslim diaspora – Somali, Sudanese, Syrian – switching between Arabic and English as easily as ordering a two-piece and Fanta Orange. Across the Middle East, North Africa and the Balkans, fried chicken has become a staple. Artist Hamja Ahsan, who visited Chicken Bazooka in 2023 as part of a project to “reclaim fried chicken” for Muslims, remembers it fondly as being “real… in a gritty sort of way.”

“Many see the rise of chicken shops, especially in the UK, as the rise of Islamification,” he has previously said. “But what these places actually offer are spaces that are beyond borders, beyond nation states, beyond ethnicities and beyond languages. Fried chicken has the power to do that.”

As autumn draws in and the day darkens, students drift down Mount Pleasant towards the city centre. Most of the men are swaddled in North Face puffers; the women wear rather less. They stop to grab a cheap meal to line their stomachs. I make an attempt at a passable chicken burger meal (you can ask for your meat to be dipped in radioactive-red chilli sauce for extra zing – we chicken out), while a vegan friend happily wolfs down his beanburger as we discuss the race politics of battered poultry, beloved of his Bajan father. “My dad couldn’t get enough KFC,” he shrugs, as he scoops up the rest of the 75p mayo. Perhaps it’s something to do with getting some flavour into the meat, he muses, or possibly because chickens were about the only livestock that were easy to farm in the Caribbean.


We observe a difficult customer testing the patience of the unflappable staff, who endure a mix of drunken banter, edgy humour and outright rudeness with weary professionalism. “I’m going to go out, get drunk and abuse a kebab shop owner,” my dining companion mutters, evoking the spirit of the angry man. The staff just keep serving.

The current proprietor, Nizar Al-Liabi, took over in 1999. Despite emails and phone calls, I never reach him. When I ask the staff, busy boxing chicken and shovelling fries, I receive a meh shrug. He can be seen on the Liverpool Echo website tearing apart a chicken fillet burger with his bare hands, but to this day I have never laid eyes on him. I think back to my days as a student, before mobile phones, to the time Al-Liabi took over. “See you outside Chicken Bazooka at 7,” was a common refrain. Everyone knew where it was – and, perhaps, some chicken while we waited. I ask my friends about their memories. “A friend got punched in there for talking favourably about a Paul Scholes goal,” offers one.


As night takes over, Chicken Bazooka becomes a beacon. The great rounded logo that once hung proudly above the door now lies shattered in the window; in my mind it rolled down Lime Street like a bowling ball, scattering hens, panhandlers and e-scooters alike. The staff greet regulars like old friends. Young men, whose night out has yielded no romantic reward, enter like cautious buffalo approaching a watering hole. Aussie mullets flirt with pastel tracksuits. A woman in a fur coat orders wings while an elderly trio from the theatre nibble wraps and incongruously sip cans of pop. Everyone ends up here eventually.

Once upon a time, this building served remedies of a different kind. For many years numbers 9–13 Ranelagh Place housed a night-and-day Boots (serving 31,000 prescriptions in the first five weeks of 1951), then a Wimpy in 1971, and subsequently, in 1994, the outlet we know today. In many ways, the building’s function hasn’t really changed; at weekends Chicken Bazooka is open eighteen hours a day.


We finish our last meal of the day – our third fried chicken meal of the day (chicken strips; a bit dry, we needed the Big Tupperware to save it) – after midnight and reflect. Chicken Bazooka may not serve especially good food. But it serves something. For some, perhaps a way to reconnect with home and heritage. For others, simply a place to eat and to work.

For all that it’s multicultural, it still feels very Scouse; the kind of messy alchemy you get when battered chicken meets hot fat. Either way, what I’ve learned over 12 hours here is that the business of the chicken is paramount. If the Liver Birds were ever to fly from their perches atop the Liver Building, some say the city would fall into the Mersey. I think the same might happen if Chicken Bazooka ever closed.

If you enjoyed this article, please share it with someone who loves (or hates) Chicken Bazooka
